lead: A three-phase voltage source inverter (VSI) has three legs, six switches and one DC bus. Each leg ties its output terminal to the positive or the negative rail. In 180° conduction every switch is gated for 180°, so three switches, one per leg, are on at every instant and the line voltage is a six-step wave. In 120° conduction each switch is gated for 120°, only two are on, and each phase has two 60° gaps. Motor drives, UPS units and solar inverters are built on this bridge.
prereq: You need: the single-phase bridge and star-delta circuit relations.

sections.h3: Three legs and the 180° switch table

blocks.text: Number the switches in the order they are gated: leg A has S1 (top) and S4 (bottom), leg B has S3 and S6, leg C has S5 and S2. In 180° mode each gate pulse is 180° wide and a new switch is gated every 60°, in the order S1, S2, S3, S4, S5, S6. The two switches of one leg are complementary, so a terminal is always tied to one rail.

In each 60° interval, two terminals share one rail and the third is on the other. For a balanced star load of R per phase, the two parallel phases (R/2) are in series with the single one, so the bus current is V<sub>dc</sub>/(1.5R). The single phase takes 2V<sub>dc</sub>/3 and each of the parallel pair V<sub>dc</sub>/3.

sections.h3: Line and phase voltages in 180° mode

blocks.text: The pole voltage v<sub>AO</sub>, measured from the bus midpoint O, is a ±V<sub>dc</sub>/2 square wave. The line voltage v<sub>AB</sub> = v<sub>AO</sub> − v<sub>BO</sub> is a quasi-square wave: +V<sub>dc</sub> for 120°, zero for 60°, −V<sub>dc</sub> for 120°, zero for 60°. The phase voltage v<sub>AN</sub> steps through V<sub>dc</sub>/3, 2V<sub>dc</sub>/3, V<sub>dc</sub>/3, −V<sub>dc</sub>/3, −2V<sub>dc</sub>/3, −V<sub>dc</sub>/3: the six-step wave.

vAB = Σ (4Vdc/nπ) cos(nπ/6) sin n(ωt + π/6) The sum runs over n = 1, 5, 7, 11, 13, …: cos(nπ/6) is zero for n = 3, 9, 15, so no triplen harmonic appears in the line or phase voltage, and the nth harmonic is 1/n of the fundamental.

blocks.text: The total rms exceeds the fundamental because of the 5th, 7th, 11th and 13th harmonics. They heat a motor and cause torque ripple; the fundamental does the useful work. Some syllabi call this bridge the six-step or square-wave VSI.

In 120° mode each gate pulse is 120° wide, still one new switch every 60°. At any instant only two switches conduct, one in the upper group and one in the lower: S6, S1 from 0° to 60°, S1, S2 from 60° to 120°, and so on. Each leg is idle for two 60° gaps per cycle, one after its top switch and one after its bottom switch. In a gap that terminal floats.

With a resistive star load the two connected phases each take V<sub>dc</sub>/2 and the floating phase takes zero. The phase voltage is +V<sub>dc</sub>/2 for 120°, zero for 60°, −V<sub>dc</sub>/2 for 120°, zero for 60°. The line voltage has no zero interval: it steps through V<sub>dc</sub>, V<sub>dc</sub>/2, −V<sub>dc</sub>/2, −V<sub>dc</sub>, −V<sub>dc</sub>/2 and V<sub>dc</sub>/2.

blocks.text: The 60° gap between the top and bottom switches of a leg makes accidental shoot-through unlikely, but it gives a lower output from the same bus and poorer switch use. With an inductive load the current of the floating phase continues through a diode of that leg, which clamps the terminal to a rail, so the voltage is no longer the ideal staircase. The conduction angle is how long a switch is gated in one cycle; it is not the firing angle of a rectifier.

Below, the phase voltage steps through 133.3, 266.7 and 133.3 volts and then the negative values; the line voltage is plus 400 volts for 120 degrees, zero for 60, minus 400 for 120 and zero for 60.

examples.question: A three-phase bridge in 180° mode has V<sub>dc</sub> = 400 V and feeds a star-connected resistive load of 10 Ω per phase. Find (a) the rms line and phase voltages, (b) the rms phase current and the load power, (c) the rms fundamental phase voltage, and (d) the peak and rms current of each switch.
steps: (d) The largest phase current flows in the single phase of each interval: 2V<sub>dc</sub>/(3R) = 2 × 400/(3 × 10) = 26.67 A. A top switch carries its phase current for half the cycle, so its rms is I<sub>P</sub>/√2 = 18.86/1.414 = 13.33 A.
examples.answer: V<sub>L</sub> = 326.6 V, V<sub>P</sub> = 188.6 V, I<sub>P</sub> = 18.86 A, P = 10.67 kW, V<sub>P1</sub> = 180.1 V; each switch carries 26.67 A peak and 13.33 A rms.

examples.question: Repeat for 120° mode with the same 400 V bus and 10 Ω star load: find the rms phase voltage and current, the power, the rms line voltage and the peak and rms switch current. Compare with 180° mode.
steps: Line voltage: two 60° steps at 400 V and four at 200 V in each cycle, so V<sub>L</sub> = √((2 × 400² + 4 × 200²)/6) = 282.8 V.
Each switch carries V<sub>dc</sub>/(2R) = 20 A for 120° of the cycle: rms = 20 × √(1/3) = 11.55 A.
Compared with 180° mode, the power falls from 10667 W to 8000 W (75 %), because each phase is connected for only two thirds of the cycle.
examples.answer: V<sub>P</sub> = 163.3 V, I<sub>P</sub> = 16.33 A, P = 8000 W, V<sub>L</sub> = 282.8 V; switch 20 A peak and 11.55 A rms; 120° mode gives 75 % of the 180° power.

traps: 180° mode does not mean both switches of a leg are on: each switch is gated for 180° and the two switches of a leg are complementary.
Keep line and phase values apart: in 180° mode the line rms is 0.816V<sub>dc</sub> and the phase rms 0.471V<sub>dc</sub>; in 120° mode 0.707V<sub>dc</sub> and 0.408V<sub>dc</sub>.
The six-step wave is the 180° phase voltage; the 180° line voltage is a 120° quasi-square. Many students swap the two sketches.
120° mode has two switches on at a time and two 60° gaps per leg per cycle, not one.
No triplen harmonics appear in a three-phase VSI line voltage; the lowest harmonics are the 5th and 7th.

quiz.q: In 180° conduction, how many switches conduct at any instant, and in what order are they gated?
quiz.a: Three, one per leg. A new switch is gated every 60° in the order S1, S2, S3, S4, S5, S6.

quiz.q: Why does the phase voltage in 180° mode take the values V<sub>dc</sub>/3 and 2V<sub>dc</sub>/3?
quiz.a: Two terminals share one rail, so their phases are in parallel (R/2) and in series with the third phase (R). The bus voltage divides 1 : 2, giving V<sub>dc</sub>/3 across each parallel phase and 2V<sub>dc</sub>/3 across the single one.

quiz.q: A 180° mode VSI has V<sub>dc</sub> = 600 V. Find the rms line voltage, the rms phase voltage and the rms fundamental line voltage.
For 120° mode with V<sub>dc</sub> = 600 V and 20 Ω per phase in star, find the rms phase current and the power.
Why is the fundamental line rms (0.780V<sub>dc</sub>) smaller than the total line rms (0.816V<sub>dc</sub>) in 180° mode?
quiz.a: The total rms adds the 5th, 7th, 11th, 13th and higher harmonics to the fundamental: √(0.816² − 0.780²) = 0.24V<sub>dc</sub> of harmonics, a THD of 31 %.

quiz.q: In 120° mode with an inductive star load, what carries the current of the floating phase during its 60° gap, and what does it do to the voltage?
quiz.a: The current keeps flowing through one of that leg's diodes, which ties the terminal to a rail until the current dies. The phase voltage then differs from the ideal staircase, so the simple 120° formulas hold only for a resistive load.

quiz.q: Give two other names for a three-phase VSI run in 180° mode.

beyond: Not for the exam. A six-step drive gives the highest fundamental a two-level bridge can make, so traction drives switch into six-step at top speed. Below that, PWM on the same bridge controls both voltage and frequency. Search for six-step operation of traction inverters and V/f control of induction motors.
